prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the development of long-acting incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single B023 part crediting Drucker, Holst and Knudsen. After the full exchange, the scientific case is stronger for me, not weaker, because no member disputes the mechanism, the maturity or the independent outcome evidence, and every dispute is about who stands in the third place and how the citation is worded. The chain is hormone physiology (Holst on secretion and incretin action, Drucker on proglucagon-derived peptide biology and therapeutic rationale), then a pharmacological solution to a half-life of minutes (Knudsen's acylation and albumin binding), then more than a decade of glycaemic, weight, cardiovascular and renal evidence from many groups. A prize for the discovery and its benefit to humankind should name both the physiology and the step that made it a medicine. Delay also carries a real cost with living laureates, as Perlmann notes. I keep a single part because splitting this into two achievements would divide one continuous line of work and spend a prize part that the remaining shortlist cannot match on combined originality and consequence.
statement.case_against: The attribution problem is real and I cannot remove it. Priority for identifying the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide is contested among Mojsov, Habener and Bell, and a three-name cap leaves out someone with a defensible claim whichever trio we pick. Naming Knudsen also means one company-based scientist represents a long industrial program, and a reviewer could read the prize as rewarding optimisation. If the committee concludes that acylation is engineering and not discovery, my trio is the weaker configuration and Perlmann's physiology-only version would be the more consistent one. I judge that acylation and albumin binding were a discovery-level design insight, but I hold that with moderate confidence.

responses.point: Perlmann holds the B023 citation to the physiology and the active peptide, names Mojsov instead of Knudsen, and says the translation is as decisive as the discovery, so excluding Knudsen is a real cost.
responses.response: Your own statement that leaving out Knudsen is a real cost is close to my argument for including her. We differ on whether the third name should be the person who identified the peptide or the person who made it usable. I keep Knudsen because her contribution is documented and not contested in the supplied record, whereas Mojsov's priority against Habener and Bell cannot be resolved from it, and I do not want a prize to settle a priority dispute by guess. I accept your point that the citation should not read as an endorsement of a product, so I have worded mine around the physiology and the development of a therapeutic class, not any compound. If the committee could document that Mojsov's work was decisive and uncontested, I would reopen the third place, but I do not think we can show that this year.

responses.point: Linnarsson moved Knudsen into his trio in place of Mojsov, calls acylation the core of what turned biology into medicine, and notes that the compound physiology-plus-industry character is the main framing risk.
responses.response: I am glad the trio now matches, and I take your point seriously that the compound character is the framing risk. I do not think it justifies two prize parts. The physiology and the drug are one continuous achievement, and each step depended on the previous one, so a split would credit the same chain twice. Your rereading of Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenboeck also reinforces my doubt about optogenetics as a second part: if omitting those three is more serious than any omission here, as you wrote to me, then B001 cannot give a defensible three-name solution this year, and I would rather leave that part unspent than force one.

responses.point: The chair says the trio changes if the prize should reward discovery and not drug design, and asks whether a second distinct achievement should share the prize, with B051 or B001 as partners.
responses.response: On your first question, the trio does depend on that choice, and my answer is that the Physiology or Medicine criterion is met by the discovery together with its consequence, so the drug-design step belongs in the citation. On the second, I do not find a partner that adds to the prize. B001 has six claimants for three places, and the medical impact is mostly as a research tool. B051 is the cleanest attribution on the list and a real conceptual advance, which is why I now list it as an alternative, but a prize that pairs it with GLP-1 would leave GLP-1 with two names and no room for Knudsen under the three-person cap. A single part with three names is the more defensible result.

responses.point: Sandberg says the third place depends on whether the core achievement is basic discovery or discovery plus development, and that B051 offers cleaner two-person credit but a smaller medical footprint.
responses.response: I agree that the third place follows from how we define the core achievement, and I think the committee should settle the definition first and the names second. The definition I propose is the physiology of GLP-1 and the creation of long-acting therapy, which gives Drucker, Holst and Knudsen. I also share your reading of B051. I have raised it in my alternatives after reading you and Linnarsson, because Mori and Walter are the best-attributed discovery on the list. I still rate it second to GLP-1 on clinical consequence, and I would not pair the two when that would cost B023 a credited name.

uncertainties: Whether acylation and albumin binding count as a discovery-level contribution or as optimisation, which decides between my trio and Perlmann's.
Whether the priority of Mojsov, Habener and Bell for identifying GLP-1(7-36) could be documented well enough to change the third place.
Whether the committee will accept a company-based development scientist alongside two academic discoverers.
Whether the division of early unfolded protein response credit between Mori and Walter holds, since Linnarsson says he is recalling it from memory.
statement.conflict_note: No candidate-specific conflict applies. I co-authored a 2009 paper with Thomas Perlmann on stem-cell-derived dopamine neurons and have worked in the same lamprey model system as Sten Grillner, but none of the shortlisted credited names (Drucker, Holst, Knudsen, Mojsov or the others) is involved in a documented tie of mine, and I propose no recusal. Optogenetics is the closest to my own field, so I have scored it on the common criteria and not on familiarity.
